title: Pulmonary tuberculosis, drug-susceptible (adult, NTEP)
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Test every presumptive TB patient upfront with NAAT (CBNAAT or Truenat) and rapid drug resistance testing, notify on Ni-kshay, triage for severe illness, and treat drug-susceptible pulmonary TB with daily 2HRZE/4HRE fixed-dose combinations by weight band, with nutrition support (Rs 1000/month), monthly review and post-treatment follow-up.

sections.title: Suspect, notify and triage
items: Presumptive TB: cough for more than 2 weeks, fever, night sweats, haemoptysis, chest pain, breathlessness, weight or appetite loss, fatigue, neck swelling, or any chest X-ray abnormality suggestive of TB.
Actively screen contacts, people with HIV, diabetes, undernutrition, smoking or alcohol use, previous TB, prisoners and other vulnerable groups.
TB is notifiable: record every diagnosed patient (public or private sector) on Ni-kshay.

Differentiated TB care: triage every patient at diagnosis and refer red-flag patients for admission. Vital-sign red flags: respiratory rate above 24/min, SpO2 below 94%, pulse above 120 or below 60/min, systolic BP below 90 mmHg.

Other red flags: BMI below 14 (or below 16 with oedema), unable to stand without support, confined to bed, breathless at rest, haemoptysis of a cup or more, altered consciousness or convulsions, jaundice, recurrent vomiting or diarrhoea.

sections.title: Diagnosis (NTEP integrated algorithm)
items: Send sputum (two specimens) for upfront NAAT (CBNAAT or Truenat) in all presumptive TB; use induced sputum or BAL if no sputum. Chest X-ray early to screen and support diagnosis.

Universal drug susceptibility testing: every diagnosed patient gets a rapid test for rifampicin resistance. If M. tuberculosis is detected and rifampicin-sensitive, test for isoniazid (and fluoroquinolone) resistance by NAAT or first-line LPA; if rifampicin resistance is detected, do second-line LPA and refer to the DR-TB centre.
New patient with low or very low M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance detected: repeat NAAT and seek microbiology advice before labelling RR-TB.
Clinically diagnosed TB (bacteriologically negative) only after alternative diagnoses are excluded; still send specimens for culture.
Baseline: HIV test, blood glucose (and HbA1c), CBC, LFT, creatinine, weight, height, BMI, SpO2, and visual acuity and colour vision before ethambutol.

sections.title: Drug-susceptible TB regimen
items: 2HRZE / 4HRE daily: intensive phase 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, then 4 months of isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol, using NTEP fixed-dose combination tablets.
Tablets daily by weight band (4FDC H75/R150/Z400/E275 mg in IP; 3FDC H75/R150/E275 mg in CP): 25 to 34 kg: 2; 35 to 49 kg: 3; 50 to 64 kg: 4; 65 to 75 kg: 5; above 75 kg: 6 (5 if 6 not tolerated).
Re-weigh monthly: change the dose if weight changes by 5 kg or more and crosses a weight band.

Take on an empty stomach where tolerated; if gastric intolerance, take with a light meal rather than stopping. Support adherence with a treatment supporter, family caregiver or digital tools (99DOTS, MERM).

Isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-sensitive TB: 6 months of levofloxacin, rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide (no separate IP or CP), extendable to 9 months. Rifampicin-resistant TB: refer to the DR-TB centre (BPaLM or shorter oral regimen).
The WHO 2022 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen is an international option; the NTEP standard remains the 6-month regimen.

sections.title: Monitoring and follow-up
items: Monthly review: symptoms, adherence, adverse drug reactions, weight and BMI, vital signs, SpO2, jaundice, oedema. Chest X-ray at the end of 2 months and as indicated.
Sputum microscopy at the end of the intensive phase (and at the end of treatment); a positive follow-up smear needs repeat drug resistance testing (NAAT, LPA or culture).

Hepatotoxicity: check LFT if anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or jaundice appear. Stop H, R and Z if ALT is more than 3 times the upper limit with symptoms or jaundice, or more than 5 times without symptoms; reintroduce drugs one at a time once LFT settle.
Ask about vision at each visit on ethambutol and stop it for blurred vision or altered colour vision.
After treatment completion, follow up every 6 months for at least 2 years to detect recurrence.

sections.title: Nutrition, social support and contacts
items: Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana: Rs 1000 per month by direct benefit transfer for the entire duration of TB or DR-TB treatment; link the bank account in Ni-kshay.
Assess nutrition at every visit; severe undernutrition (BMI below 16 with oedema, haemoglobin below 7 g/dL, MUAC below 16 cm) may need admission. Offer linkage to Ni-kshay Mitra community support.
Trace and screen all household contacts; offer TB preventive treatment once active TB is excluded (see TB preventive treatment protocol).
Advise cough hygiene, ventilation, and smoking and alcohol cessation.

sections.title: Special situations
items: HIV: start ATT first, then antiretroviral therapy as early as tolerated (usually within 2 weeks) except in TB meningitis where it is delayed; give co-trimoxazole prophylaxis; watch for IRIS and rifampicin-ART interactions.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: H, R, Z and E are safe; avoid aminoglycosides; continue breastfeeding. Give vitamin K to newborns of mothers on rifampicin.
CKD (creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min): no change for rifampicin and isoniazid; give pyrazinamide and ethambutol three times a week (not daily), after dialysis on dialysis days.
Chronic liver disease: fewer hepatotoxic drugs according to Child-Pugh class (e.g. Child A: 9 months HRE; Child C: no hepatotoxic drugs); manage with a specialist.

Rifampicin reduces levels of hormonal contraceptives, warfarin, many antiretrovirals, anticonvulsants and steroids; advise barrier contraception. Diabetes: screen all patients and optimise glucose control.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating 'non-resolving pneumonia' with fluoroquinolones, which masks TB and delays diagnosis.
Starting ATT without NAAT and rifampicin resistance testing, or without Ni-kshay notification.
Missing red flags at diagnosis: most early TB deaths occur in severely ill, undernourished patients who were not admitted.
Not changing the weight band as the patient gains weight, or stopping treatment when symptoms settle.

drugs.name: 4FDC HRZE (isoniazid 75 mg, rifampicin 150 mg, pyrazinamide 400 mg, ethambutol 275 mg)
drugs.dose: Orally once daily for 2 months: 25 to 34 kg 2 tablets; 35 to 49 kg 3; 50 to 64 kg 4; 65 to 75 kg 5; above 75 kg 6
drugs.notes: Approximates H 5, R 10, Z 25, E 15 mg/kg/day.

drugs.name: 3FDC HRE (isoniazid 75 mg, rifampicin 150 mg, ethambutol 275 mg)
drugs.dose: Orally once daily for 4 months, same number of tablets as in the intensive phase
drugs.notes: Adjust band if weight changes by 5 kg or more.

drugs.name: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6)
drugs.dose: 10 to 25 mg orally once daily with isoniazid
drugs.notes: For those at risk of neuropathy: diabetes, alcohol use, undernutrition, HIV, CKD, pregnancy, breastfeeding.

drugs.name: H mono/poly-resistant regimen (6)Lfx-REZ
drugs.dose: Daily for 6 months. 30 to 45 kg: rifampicin 450 mg, ethambutol 800 mg, pyrazinamide 1250 mg, levofloxacin 750 mg. 46 to 70 kg: 600 mg, 1200 mg, 1750 mg, 1000 mg. Above 70 kg: 750 mg, 1600 mg, 2000 mg, 1000 mg
drugs.notes: Only after rifampicin resistance is excluded; extend to 9 months for extensive disease or month-4 smear positive (NTEP DR-TB 2025).
